newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia to hold unprecedented re-vote on island.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia to hold unprecedented re-vote on island.

text.p: Indonesia prepared to run an unprecedented re-vote on an island off East Java while a minority party said on Tuesday it might have to quit parliament after a disastrous showing in last week's general elections.

Electoral officers said there would be a re-vote on Wednesday at 86 polling stations at Sampang on Madura island after a crowd alleging election rigging burned the ballot boxes from last Thursday's polls.

Political analysts said a re-vote was unprecedented in Indonesian election history, and some questioned whether such a move might encourage future voters angered by poll results to stage similar attacks.
The Sampang secretary of the Moslem-backed United Development Party (PPP), Hasan Asy'ari, said his party wanted a re-vote throughout the Sampang regency, not just at the 86 stations.
PPP supporters in the devoutly Moslem area rioted after polls closed on Thursday alleging the vote had been rigged in favour of the ruling Golkar party.

Golkar swept the national vote with a record 74 percent, with the PPP on just under 23 percent. The only other legal party, the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), saw its vote share plunge to three percent.

PDI deputy chairman Harsoko Sudiro said his party might have to withdraw from the House of Representatives as under parliamentary rules it had to have individual members for all 11 house commissions. It only got 10 members last Thursday, compared to 56 in the previous parliament.
The PPP's Asy'ari told Reuters: "Our witnesses saw irregularities and violations of election rules in all the polling stations." He added that the PPP would not supply witnesses for the re-vote.
PPP officials in Jakarta have also spoken of widespread irregularities and are due to meet on Thursday to decide whether to accept the election result.
Financial markets were steady on Tuesday, with the stock index down slightly on profit-taking.
But economic analysts are keeping a wary eye on Thursday's PPP meeting after clashes between partisans of the PPP and Golkar produced the most violent election campaign in three decades.
President Suharto, in power for the past 30 years, has based the country's politics on a three-party system created in the early 1970s.
Mohammad Hikam, a political scientist at the Indonesian Academy of Sciences, said he believed the government would intervene to prevent a PDI withdrawal from the 500-seat House of Representatives.
"I don't think the government will allow such a thing to happen...or maybe the House will have to change its internal regulations if the PDI does quit," he said.

The PDI collapse to three percent of the vote from 15 percent in the last elections in 1992 followed the ousting of the party's popular leader Megawati Sukarnoputri by a government-backed faction last year.
